newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ GDP data seen endorsing expected RBNZ easing.
newsitem.headline: NZ GDP data seen endorsing expected RBNZ easing.

text.p: New Zealand Gross Domestic Product data for the March quarter should reflect a flat economy and endorse the Reserve Bank's expected easing of monetary conditions, economists said on Wednesday.
But the data, to be released on Monday, would be closely watched for any divergence from the central bank's GDP forecasts in its Monetary Policy Statement (MPS) on Friday.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expect seasonally adjusted, production based GDP to come in at -0.09 percent for the March quarter for a 1.93 percent rise in the year to March.
"So obviously a very weak quarter, the weakest one we've had since I can't remember when," said ANZ economist Bernard Hodgetts.
"I guess the significance of that is it confirms that things really have come off the boil in the last six to 12 months."
The Reserve Bank is widely expected to sanction an easing in monetary conditions on Friday because of the relative absence of inflationary pressures in the current low-growth environment.

"So if you got a GDP number that came out at zero (for the quarter), basically that would be entirely consistent with what people are building into their thinking, and I would have thought the reaction to that would be either neutral or slightly positive from a bond market point of view," said Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek.
He said the GDP numbers would have to be significantly at odds with the RBNZ's forecast for the market to react fiercely.

With all indicators pointing to a sluggish economy, and in anticipation of a looser stance from the central bank, financial markets have already eased monetary conditions well below the RBNZ's desired levels in its March statement.
BNZ economist Peter Jolly said he expected the bank to be more cautious in its MPS than the GDP data would suggest it needed to be.

"Certainly our longer term view is that no matter what the bank says on Friday -- and we expect them to be more hawkish than most people think -- that monetary conditions are going to ease a lot anyway," he said.
But the GDP data was unlikely to alter the wider picture painted by the Reserve Bank's statement and the coalition government's first budget, to be delivered on Thursday.
Low growth is expected to see the 1997/98 budget surplus forecast slashed to half the NZ$3.3 billion predicted in March.

"And we're expectating that the Reserve Bank is going to reduce its growth forecast in the year to March 1998, just based on the soft economic indicators and the business confidence surveys, which say that growth isn't likely to pick up anytime soon," Bennenbroek added.
Economists noted GDP statistics, while a definitive indicator of economic growth, were nevertheless historical.
"Unfortunately, the GDP releases in New Zealand are always so late that they never really do change people's views," said Hodgetts.
He said the financial markets would take more notice of the GDP data if they were more timely.
Statistics New Zealand said it was working to improve the timeliness of the release, but any gains were unlikely to be made within the next 12 months.
